title: Navratri 2026 Day 1: The Bollywood Garba Tracks to Open Nine Nights of Dancing
excerpt: From the soulful "Shubhaarambh" opener to the timeless "Dholi Taro Dhol Baaje" closer, here is the Day 1 playlist that carries a garba night from dusk to midnight.
body:
• Sharad Navratri begins Sunday, October 11, 2026, with Day 1 dedicated to Maa Shailputri. The opening night sets the tone for nine nights of garba and dandiya, so the first playlist of the season matters most.
  • Start with the soulful "Shubhaarambh" from Kai Po Che!, then build through modern anthems "Chogada," "Kamariya," and "Dholida" before peak-hour "Nagada Sang Dhol" brings the loudest ten minutes of the night.
  • Close every set with the 1999 classic "Dholi Taro Dhol Baaje" from Hum Dil De Chuke Sanam. Twenty-seven years on, it remains the most requested garba track at diaspora events.
  • Reader utility: download your playlist offline on Spotify, JioSaavn, or Apple Music before heading to a community-hall garba. Venue Wi-Fi almost always buckles after 10 PM, and most US garba events run 7 PM to midnight.

The opening night sets the season

Day 1 of Sharad Navratri honors Maa Shailputri, the first form of Goddess Durga, and it carries a weight the other eight nights do not. In Ahmedabad the grounds fill at dusk; in community halls from Edison to Leicester, the first circle of dancers forms a little after seven. Whatever plays first becomes the reference point for the next nine nights, according to LatestLY, which published its Navratri 2026 playlist on October 11 to mark the festival's start. A strong Day 1 list needs an arc: devotional openers, a slow build, two hours of peak energy, and one song that everyone knows by heart.

The first hour: ease them in

Begin with "Shubhaarambh" from Kai Po Che! (2013). Composed and sung by Amit Trivedi with Divya Kumar and Shruti Pathak, with lyrics by Swanand Kirkire, the track is literally about auspicious beginnings. It is the rare festival song that works at conversation volume, which is exactly what the first hour needs while latecomers arrive and the circles are still forming. Follow it with "Udi Udi Jaye" from Raees (2017), composed by Ram Sampath and sung by Sukhwinder Singh, Bhoomi Trivedi, and Karsan Sagathia, with lyrics by Javed Akhtar. Shah Rukh Khan and Mahira Khan's kite-flying number was filmed for Makar Sankranti, but its Gujarati folk pulse makes it a natural Navratri opener.

Peak hours: the modern anthems

Once the floor is full, the playlist belongs to the 2010s. "Chogada" from Loveyatri (2018), sung by Darshan Raval and Asees Kaur, became the garba anthem of its release year and has never left the rotation since. "Kamariya" from Mitron (2018), also fronted by Darshan Raval, brings the same high-voltage energy with Jackky Bhagnani and Kritika Kamra on screen. Then comes Alia Bhatt's showstopper: "Dholida" from Gangubai Kathiawadi (2022), composed by Sanjay Leela Bhansali, sung by Janhvi Shrimankar and Shail Hada, and choreographed by Kruti Mahesh. Its raw power makes it the centerpiece of any serious garba set. Save "Nagada Sang Dhol Baaje" from Goliyon Ki Raasleela Ram-Leela (2013) for the loudest ten minutes of the night. Bhansali's composition, sung by Shreya Ghoshal and Osman Mir with lyrics by Siddharth-Garima, and picturized on Deepika Padukone, Ranveer Singh, and Supriya Pathak, is the closest thing this generation has to a folk standard.

The classic closer

End with "Dholi Taro Dhol Baaje" from Hum Dil De Chuke Sanam (1999). Ismail Darbar's composition, sung by Kavita Krishnamurthy, Vinod Rathod, and Karsan Sargathia with lyrics by Mehboob, and picturized on Salman Khan and Aishwarya Rai, has outlasted every trend cycle for nearly three decades. DJs report it is still the one track that pulls grandparents onto the floor. Nothing signals the night is ending quite like it.

The diaspora angle

For Indian families abroad, the playlist is also an organizer. NRI Globe's Navratri 2026 guide notes that diaspora events typically move through three phases: a devotional opening with aartis, a Falguni Pathak block for the elders, and a Bollywood-heavy peak for mixed crowds. Families in New Jersey, Dubai, and Sydney often add regional numbers, from Maharashtrian devotional tracks to Rajasthani folk, when the crowd is mixed. The guide's practical advice holds everywhere: build the playlist this week, test the sequence once at home, and share one link with your local temple or association so everyone dances to the same order.

What's next

Nine nights, nine forms of the goddess, one dance floor. Navratri runs through October 19, closing with Dussehra on October 20, 2026. Night 4 honors Maa Kushmanda, Night 6 peaks for Maa Katyayani, and Night 9 closes with Maa Siddhidatri, and veteran organizers rotate the mood each night: devotional-heavy early, folk in the middle, all-out Bollywood at the end. Start with this Day 1 list tonight, and the rest of the festival takes care of itself.
